questions.q: Which description of digital video matches the lecture?
choices: A single compressed image plus a list of motion vectors
A continuous analog signal sampled once per second
A sequence of images (frames) displayed at a constant rate, e.g. 24 or 30 images/sec, each an array of pixels
A stream of pixels sent at whatever rate the network allows, with no fixed frame rate
questions.explain: Video is a sequence of images shown at a constant rate (e.g., 24 or 30 frames/sec). Each digital image is an array of pixels, and each pixel is represented by bits.

questions.q: A run of N identical purple sky pixels is sent as just two values: the color (purple) and the repeat count N. What kind of coding is this?
choices: Temporal coding
Spatial coding
Variable bit rate transmission
DASH chunking
questions.explain: Spatial coding uses redundancy within a single image. Here it replaces N repeated values with two.

questions.q: A frame has a run of 500 identical purple pixels. With the spatial coding trick from the lecture, how many values are needed to encode that run?
questions.explain: Two values: the color and the number of repeats. The run length (500) doesn't change that.

questions.q: Instead of sending the complete frame i+1, an encoder sends only the differences from frame i. What does this exploit?
choices: Redundancy within a single image (spatial)
The constant bit rate of the encoder
Redundancy between consecutive images (temporal)
The client's playout buffer
questions.explain: Temporal coding uses redundancy from one image to the next. If a frame barely changes, only the changes need to be sent.

questions.q: In constant bit rate (CBR) video, the encoding rate rises and falls as the amount of spatial and temporal redundancy in the scene changes.
questions.explain: That describes variable bit rate (VBR). In CBR, the video encoding rate is fixed.

questions.q: A VBR-encoded video switches between a nearly static talking-head shot and a fast-moving action scene. Which part most likely needs the higher encoding rate, and why?
choices: The talking head, because static frames contain more pixels
Both need the same rate, because VBR fixes the rate per video
The talking head, because temporal coding works poorly when nothing changes
The action scene, because frames change a lot, so there's less temporal redundancy to exploit
questions.explain: VBR's rate changes with the amount of spatial and temporal coding possible. When consecutive frames differ a lot, sending only the differences saves little, so more bits are needed.

questions.q: Which encoding standard is often used on the Internet, with rates from about 64 Kbps to 12 Mbps?
choices: MPEG 1
MPEG 2
MPEG 4
HTTP/2
questions.explain: MPEG4 covers 64 Kbps to 12 Mbps and is often used on the Internet. MPEG 1 (CD-ROM) is about 1.5 Mbps, and MPEG2 (DVD) is 3-6 Mbps.

questions.q: Which challenges do large-scale video streaming services face?
choices: Scale: reaching on the order of a billion users
Heterogeneity: users differ (wired vs. mobile, bandwidth-rich vs. bandwidth-poor)
No standard video compression exists
Every viewer needs a dedicated circuit through the network
questions.explain: The two challenges are scale and heterogeneity. The answer to both is a distributed, application-level infrastructure.

questions.q: What is the general solution to the scale and heterogeneity challenges of video streaming?
choices: Reserving bandwidth for each stream in the network-core routers
A distributed, application-level infrastructure
One very large server at a central location
Replacing packet switching with circuit switching
questions.explain: Streaming services build distributed infrastructure at the application level (for example, CDNs plus client-driven DASH) on top of the existing Internet.

questions.q: In the three-step picture (1. video recorded, 2. video sent, 3. video received and played out), what makes this 'streaming'?
choices: The server sends at exactly the rate the video was recorded
The network delay is fixed
The video is recorded at 30 frames/sec
The client plays out early parts of the video while the server is still sending later parts
questions.explain: Streaming means playout starts before the whole video has arrived. For example, the client plays frame 2 while the server sends frame 10.

questions.q: Compared with downloading a whole video before playing it, what advantages does streaming offer?
choices: Playout can begin earlier
Less bandwidth is wasted if the viewer doesn't watch the whole video
Network delay becomes constant
No client-side buffer is needed
questions.explain: Streaming lets playout start sooner and avoids sending parts that are never watched. It doesn't remove variable delay, so the client still needs a buffer.

questions.q: Which of these are challenges in streaming stored video?
choices: Server-to-client bandwidth varies with congestion (in the home, access network, network core, or video server)
Network delays vary (jitter)
Client interactivity: pause, fast-forward, rewind, jumping through the video
Lost video packets may be retransmitted, adding delay
The recorded frame rate changes randomly during playout
questions.explain: The main challenges are varying bandwidth and variable delay/loss. Other challenges are interactivity and retransmission of lost packets. The recorded frame rate is fixed by the recording.

questions.q: What does the continuous playout constraint say?
choices: Once client playout starts, playout timing must match the original recording timing
The server must transmit at exactly the playout rate
Every frame must take the same network path
The client must download the whole video before playing it
questions.explain: During playout, each frame must be played at its original time. Network delays vary, though, so the client needs a buffer to meet this constraint.

questions.q: What is the term for variation in network delay from one packet or frame to the next?
questions.explain: Jitter is variable network delay. Client-side buffering absorbs it.

questions.q: What are client-side buffering and an initial playout delay used for?
choices: Increasing the available bandwidth on the path
Choosing the encoding rate of the next chunk
Compensating for network-added delay and delay jitter
Reducing the number of bits per frame
questions.explain: The client waits, builds up a buffer, and then plays at the original timing, even though frames arrive unevenly.

questions.q: At time t, a client has received chunks 1 through 9 and has played out chunks 1 through 3. How many chunks are in its playout buffer?
questions.explain: Buffered = received - played out = 9 - 3 = 6. (On the slide, at t0, 6 received - 2 played = 4 buffered.)

questions.q: A client sets a very short initial playout delay, and frame delays are highly variable. What is the most likely result?
choices: A frame misses its playout time (starvation), and the video freezes with a 'buffering' spinner
The viewer waits a long time before the video starts
The server automatically lowers its encoding rate
Frames are played faster than their original timing to catch up
questions.explain: With too little buffered, a late frame isn't there when it's needed. That is starvation, and the video freezes.

questions.q: What is the downside of a very long initial playout delay?
choices: Starvation becomes more likely
The client has to request lower-quality chunks
Frames are played out of their original timing
The viewer waits longer before playout begins
questions.explain: A longer delay protects against starvation, but users don't like waiting. Picking the delay means balancing the two.

questions.q: On a plot of cumulative data vs. time for client video reception (with variable network delay), what does an unusually long horizontal step mean?
choices: The encoder produced an unusually large frame
That frame's network delay was much longer than the previous frame's
The client paused playout
The server stopped recording
questions.explain: A horizontal segment means time passes with no new data. Long steps mean a frame arrived much later than the one before it, and short steps mean it arrived much sooner.

questions.q: Playout buffering alone can keep video playing smoothly even if the available bandwidth stays below the video's encoding rate for a long time.
questions.explain: Buffering absorbs variable delay. A long bandwidth shortfall drains the buffer, so the client has to lower the rate, which is what DASH is for.

questions.q: What does DASH stand for?
questions.explain: DASH is Dynamic, Adaptive Streaming over HTTP.

questions.q: Which problem is DASH mainly designed to handle, as opposed to playout buffering?
choices: Variable network delay (jitter)
Available server-to-client bandwidth that changes over time or is too low for the current rate
Spatial redundancy within frames
Packet reordering inside routers
questions.explain: Buffering absorbs variable delay. DASH adapts the encoding rate (and server) to the available bandwidth.

questions.q: In DASH, which of these does the server side do?
choices: Divides the video file into multiple chunks
Encodes each chunk at multiple different rates
Stores the different rate encodings in different files, replicated across CDN nodes
Provides a manifest file with URLs for the different chunks
Measures each client's bandwidth and picks its encoding rate
Pushes chunks to the client at a fixed rate, whether or not they're requested
questions.explain: The server prepares chunks, encodings, files, replicas, and the manifest. The client estimates bandwidth, picks the rate, and requests each chunk.

questions.q: What does the DASH manifest file contain?
choices: The video itself at its highest encoding rate
The client's bandwidth history, reported back to the server
URLs for the different chunks (each encoding and where it is stored)
The DNS record of the origin server only
questions.explain: The manifest lists the client's options: each chunk, at each encoding rate, and the servers/URLs it can be fetched from.

questions.q: In DASH, the 'intelligence' is at the client. Which decisions does the client make?
choices: When to request a chunk (so the buffer doesn't starve or overflow)
What encoding rate to request
Where to request the chunk from (e.g., a nearby server or one with high available bandwidth)
How the server divides the video into chunks
Which set of encoding rates the server produces
questions.explain: The client decides when, at what rate, and from where. Chunking and the available encodings are set up on the server side.

questions.q: A DASH manifest offers each chunk at 1, 2.5, 5, and 8 Mbps. The client estimates 6 Mbps of available server-to-client bandwidth. What rate (in Mbps) should it request for the next chunk?
questions.explain: The client picks the highest encoding rate it can sustain with the current bandwidth. 8 Mbps is more than 6 Mbps, so it picks 5 Mbps.

questions.q: Partway through a stream, a DASH client's bandwidth estimate drops sharply. What typically happens?
choices: For the next chunk, the client requests a lower-rate encoding (and may choose a different server)
The server notices the congestion and re-encodes the current chunk
The client restarts from the first chunk at a lower rate
TCP automatically switches the connection to a lower encoding
questions.explain: Rates are chosen one chunk at a time by the client, so it can step down for the next request without restarting.

questions.q: Within one DASH session, the client must request every chunk at the same encoding rate from the same server.
questions.explain: The client can pick different rates at different times, based on the bandwidth available then, and can fetch from different servers.

questions.q: A higher-quality encoding of a chunk is stored in a larger file and needs more bandwidth to download in time.
questions.explain: Higher quality means more bits per chunk, so a larger file and a higher required rate.

questions.q: Complete the summary: Streaming video = encoding + DASH + ________.
questions.explain: Streaming video = encoding + DASH + playout buffering.

questions.q: Why doesn't a single, large 'mega-server' work for streaming to hundreds of thousands of simultaneous users?
choices: It is a single point of failure
It is a point of network congestion
Distant clients have long (and possibly congested) paths to it
It cannot use HTTP
It cannot store more than one encoding of a video
questions.explain: Single point of failure, congestion point, and long paths to far-away clients: this approach doesn't scale.

questions.q: What does a content distribution network (CDN) do?
choices: Sends all requests to one central data center
Reserves a dedicated circuit for each viewer
Encodes each video once, at a single rate
Stores and serves multiple copies of videos at multiple geographically distributed sites
questions.explain: A CDN is option 2: replicate content at many distributed sites so clients can be served from nearby copies.

questions.q: Which describes the 'enter deep' CDN approach?
choices: A small number (tens) of large clusters in POPs near access networks
Pushing CDN servers deep into many access networks, close to users
Putting all servers deep inside a single data center
Routing every request through the network core to an origin server
questions.explain: Enter deep puts servers inside many access networks at the Internet's edge, close to users.

questions.q: Which describes the 'bring home' CDN approach?
choices: Servers inside nearly every access network
Caching video only on users' home devices
A smaller number (tens) of larger clusters in POPs near access networks
One mega-server located near the content owner
questions.explain: Bring home uses fewer, larger server clusters in points of presence (POPs) near access networks.

questions.q: Which pairing of CDN company and approach is correct?
choices: Akamai: enter deep; Limelight: bring home
Akamai: bring home; Limelight: enter deep
Both use enter deep
Both use bring home
questions.explain: Akamai pushes many servers deep into access networks (about 240,000 servers in over 120 countries in 2015). Limelight uses bring home.

questions.q: Compared with enter deep, the bring home approach puts CDN servers in many more locations, closer to users.
questions.explain: It's the opposite. Bring home uses fewer (tens of) larger clusters in POPs. Enter deep uses many servers inside access networks, close to users.

questions.q: How can a client be directed to the CDN server that holds the content it requested?
choices: A manifest file
A CDN DNS server
The client's home router broadcasts the location
A mega-server relays all of the traffic
questions.explain: Either a manifest file or a CDN DNS server points the client to the content.

questions.q: Which sequence matches how a Netflix client streams an episode?
choices: Client fetches chunks from a random CDN node, then asks Netflix for a manifest to check them
Netflix pushes the whole episode to the client, which then picks a rate
Client requests the content from Netflix; Netflix returns a manifest; client fetches chunks from a CDN node at the highest supportable rate; it may switch rate or copy if the path gets congested
Client's ISP picks the CDN node and rate, then tells Netflix which manifest to send
questions.explain: The subscriber asks, the provider returns a manifest, and then the client, using DASH, retrieves chunks from CDN nodes and adapts its rate and server choice as conditions change.

questions.q: Netflix stores copies of its content at the nodes of its own worldwide CDN. What is that CDN called?
questions.explain: Netflix's CDN is OpenConnect.

questions.q: What does it mean to call Netflix an OTT ('over the top') service?
choices: It operates its own ISP and access network to reach subscribers
It is an application-level service that delivers content over ISPs' networks, using Internet host-to-host communication as a service, without being an ISP
It sends video over dedicated circuits that bypass the Internet
It runs above the transport layer only in the network core
questions.explain: Netflix is about content, not the network. It runs at the application layer on top of the IP infrastructure that ISPs provide.

questions.q: OTT services have to cope with a congested Internet from the 'edge'. Which of these are OTT challenges?
choices: What content to place in which CDN node
Which CDN node to retrieve content from
What rate to retrieve content at
Configuring routers inside ISPs' core networks
Assigning IP addresses to subscribers
questions.explain: An OTT service controls only its own servers and clients. It can't configure ISP routers or addressing, so it decides placement, server selection, and rate.

questions.q: While a Netflix episode is playing, the path to the client's current CDN server becomes congested. What can the client do?
choices: Ask Netflix to reroute the ISP's traffic around the congestion
Nothing; it must wait until the path clears
Download the rest of the episode from Netflix's central servers
Request the next chunks from a different copy listed in the manifest, possibly at a different rate
questions.explain: The manifest lists several copies and rates, so the client can switch to another CDN server and/or rate for the next chunk.

questions.q: OTT services like Netflix reflect the view of the Internet as a service infrastructure that applications are built on.
questions.explain: Besides the 'nuts and bolts' view, the Internet can be seen as infrastructure that provides services to applications. OTT services build on that host-to-host service.
